summary: Proposes a generic architecture for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA): a general AAA server that application-specific modules can plug into. It is experimental and sets out a design rather than a finished protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2903 proposes a shared server for the three checks that access systems make: confirming who a user is, deciding what the user may do, and recording what was used. The server applies general rules, and a separate module holds the knowledge of each particular application.

questions: how does generic aaa server work
how to do multi domain authorization
what is the generic aaa server
subtitle: One server for the checks every access system makes, with the details of each application left to a plug-in module.

tldr.problem: Every application that restricts, charges for or records access needs the same three checks: who the user is, what the user may use, and what was used. Building a separate system for each application repeats the same work.
tldr.mechanism: The memo puts the shared checks in a generic AAA server that applies rules to a request, and leaves the details of each application to an Application Specific Module reached through a named interface.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental memo that sets out a design rather than a finished protocol. The authors call it a starting point for further work, and it asks for discussion and suggestions for improvement.

facts.label: Components of a generic AAA server

today: RFC 2903 is an Experimental document from August 2000, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo describes itself as work in progress, so what it defines is a set of ideas for building a shared AAA infrastructure rather than a protocol an implementation can follow today.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2903 comes from the Authorization subgroup of the IETF's AAA Working Group, and later from the AAAarch Research Group in the IRTF. The authors describe it as a starting point for further work, published so that others can build on it, and not as a definitive description of architecture or requirements.

The proposal is a network of cooperating generic AAA servers that speak a common protocol. A request can combine authorizations of different types in one transaction, and the infrastructure forwards each part of the request to the AAA server able to decide it, then collects the answers. Because each application has needs of its own, the memo adds an application interface between the generic server and a set of Application Specific Modules that carry out the work only that application knows how to do.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo offers an early design for shared access control. It asks for comments rather than claiming a finished protocol, so read the details as a proposal to build on.

sections.title: The Components of a Generic AAA Server
sections.content:
Section 2.1 lists five components. The authorization rule evaluation engine is the core: it receives a request, inspects it and decides. It knows the logic and understands some general information, but nothing about application specifics except where those can be evaluated to a boolean or numerical value. That lets a rule refer to data elements nobody considered when the application was created, such as a request for a remote virtual control room experiment that succeeds only if a dial-in access server allows it, a bandwidth broker has capacity available, and the experimenter has the money to pay for it.

The Application Specific Module, written ASM in the memo, is a separate component that holds the knowledge of one application. In a service provider it manages resources and configures the service equipment, and it may also take part in the decision. Because it is a separate component it must be addressable, so it needs a place in a global naming space. The authorization event log stores time-stamped events for auditing, and the log can also be used as input to rules, so that an authorization is given only if some other event was logged in the past. With the aid of certificates, the log could support non-repudiation. The policy repository holds the available services and resources, together with the policy rules used to decide about them. Request forwarding carries messages between AAA servers, and the memo says the protocol used for that should be peer to peer.
sections.plainLanguage: The server has five parts: a rule engine that decides, a module for each application's special knowledge, a log of past decisions, a store of rules, and a way to pass requests to other servers. Each of them needs names that work across organizations.

sections.title: How the Server Handles a Request
sections.content:
With those components in place, the server inspects a request, works out which authorization is being asked for, retrieves the rules from the repository, performs its local functions, and then chooses one of three ways to handle each part of the request: let an attached Application Specific Module evaluate it, look up the answer in the event log or the policy repository, or forward the part to another AAA server for evaluation.

The memo draws three kinds of link around the server, numbered by type. Type 1 is the future AAA protocol, used between AAA servers. Type 2 is the link to the application, which must support a global naming space for application specific items. Type 3 is the link to the policy and event repository, which has the same requirement. A separate gateway function can carry legacy protocols: it wraps old protocol data units inside the new protocol's messages, so that RADIUS attribute value pairs travel as Application Specific Information units that can be signed and encrypted between a service provider's AAA server and a home AAA server that talk to each other through a proxy neither fully trusts. The communication between a module and the service equipment is a fifth type, and it is specific to the service.
sections.plainLanguage: For each part of a request the server picks one of three routes: ask the module for that application, look it up in its own records, or pass it to another server. The server talks over three kinds of link, numbered 1 to 3, plus a fourth for older protocols and a fifth to the service itself.

sections.title: The Layered AAA Protocol Model
sections.content:
Section 3 explores organizing the AAA functions as four service layers: Application Specific Service Layer, Presentation Service Layer, Transaction/Session Management Service Layer, and Reliable/Secure Transport Service Layer. Each layer holds a set of distributed processes that cooperate, and each uses a protocol specialized for the job assigned to that layer. A layer depends on the services of the layer below it and has its own end point address space, so the layers assemble into a protocol stack.

The stated benefit is that there is no single monolithic AAA protocol but a suite of them, each optimized for a narrow problem. The protocol at a layer can be substituted for a functionally equivalent one without disrupting the layers above it, so local security requirements can change the transport layer without the layers above noticing. The protocol for a layer is simpler because it is focused, and existing designs can be reused, for example CORBA GIOP and CDR for the presentation layer. A legacy message such as a RADIUS message can be carried inside the lower layer's messages. The memo adds that the interface between the generic server and the modules may be more complicated than a simple layered model allows, and that the layering is not offered as a reference model ready for protocol design.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo splits the work across four layers instead of one large protocol. Each layer has its own job and its own protocol, and a layer can be replaced without disturbing the layers above it. The authors call this an organizing idea, not a finished model.

sections.title: The Transaction and Session Management Layer
sections.content:
The AAA Transaction/Session Management layer, written AAA-TSM in the memo, is the set of AAA servers that collectively provide three services. Authentication confirms the identity of the other parties with which the entity has a trust relationship. Authorization decides whether a user gets the services or resources asked for: when the request is instantaneous and transient its approval is an ephemeral transaction, and when the approval implies sustained use of a service or resources the request becomes an Authorized Session whose distributed state the layer keeps in step across every server involved. Accounting generates information about the authorization decision and about any ongoing session.

The layer routes a request from one stakeholder to the next, accumulating approvals until everyone has been asked. Any stakeholder on the consent list can veto, and the servers that had already approved are then told to cancel their reservations. Each request message carries its own context state so that a server can act on it without further exchanges. The memo lists what that state may hold: a session identifier; permission lists saying which servers may change which parts; the user's authorization request encoded as a presentation layer PDU; authentication information such as an X.509 public key certificate; credentials, or a pointer to where they can be found; the list of stakeholders not yet visited, each with instructions on how the request should be evaluated; the current position in that list; the list of servers that have conditionally approved, each with a digital signature so the approval can be verified later; an expiration time stamp, which also limits replay; an audit trail of which parties changed the request terms; and an integrity check computed over the whole message.
sections.plainLanguage: This layer confirms identity, decides access and records use. It passes a request from one organization to the next until all have answered, and it keeps a full description of the request inside each message so a server can act without asking more questions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations section points back to the AAA Authorization Framework and to the application examples for the security requirements of the framework and for the authorization requirements. It then makes one proposal of its own: a base AAA protocol should define a standard set of security mechanisms, including public key encryption and digital signatures, that can be applied to individual information units inside an AAA message. That granularity is needed for end-to-end security, because a single AAA message may contain information units each generated by AAA servers from different administrative domains and destined for AAA servers in different domains.

The memo also notes that encrypting or signing an entire message hop by hop may be necessary, and that this could be handled by a standard lower layer protocol such as IPSEC. If it is, then auditing has to meet certain requirements, so that it can be established later that the messages relating to a specific session were protected in a particular way. Alternatively, hop-by-hop security mechanisms may be built into the base AAA protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo wants each piece of information in a message to be signed or encrypted separately, because one message can travel across several organizations. Whole-message protection can be added on each hop, either by IPSEC or by the AAA protocol itself.

viz.caption: THE FIVE COMPONENTS OF A GENERIC AAA SERVER

items.title: Rule evaluation engine
items.text: Inspects the request and decides, using logic and general information it understands.

items.title: Application Specific Module
items.text: A separate component holding what one application knows; it must be addressable.

items.title: Authorization event log
items.text: Stores time-stamped events for auditing, and can feed later rules.

items.title: Policy repository
items.text: Holds the available services and resources and the rules about them.

items.title: Request forwarding
items.text: Passes messages between AAA servers over a peer-to-peer protocol.

messages.label: AUTHORIZATION REQUEST
messages.note: One request that needs several approvals.

messages.label: DIAL-IN ACCESS
messages.note: Does the network access server allow it?

messages.label: FUNDS
messages.note: Does the experimenter have the money to pay?

viz.caption: THE FOUR AAA SERVICE LAYERS, TOP TO BOTTOM

layers.label: Application Specific Service Layer
layers.detail: The logic of one application, and the rules it needs.

layers.label: Presentation Service Layer
layers.detail: Encodes data so that peers on different systems can read it.

layers.label: AAA Transaction/Session Management Service Layer
layers.detail: Authentication, authorization and accounting across cooperating servers.

layers.label: Reliable/Secure Transport Service Layer
layers.detail: Carries the messages and protects each hop.
